title: ItsDangerous: How a Token Is Built and Torn Apart
premise: You want to hand a piece of data to someone you don't trust — a browser cookie, a URL in an activation email, a form field — and get it back later knowing nobody changed it. You can't hide the data, and you don't want to store a copy server-side. The only thing you have that the other side doesn't is a secret key. ItsDangerous is the small library that turns that secret into a tamper-evident wrapper: it serializes an object to bytes, appends a keyed signature, and refuses to give the object back unless the signature still matches — optionally checking how old the token is, and optionally squeezing it into characters that are safe in a URL. This story follows a single token from the object you pass in, down through serialization, compression, timestamping, key derivation and HMAC, and back up again through verification and failure handling.

chapters.title: A Dot in the Middle
inputs: Nothing; this is the entry point
facts: `src/itsdangerous/__init__.py` is nothing but re-exports: every public name (`Serializer`, `Signer`, `TimestampSigner`, `TimedSerializer`, `URLSafeSerializer`, `URLSafeTimedSerializer`, the six exceptions, and three encoding helpers) is imported with the `X as X` idiom so type checkers treat them as exported.

The README's example shows the whole contract: `URLSafeSerializer('secret key', 'auth').dumps({...})` produces `eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9.6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg`, and `loads` returns the original dict.
Every token has the same shape: payload, a separator (default `.`), then a signature; the payload is readable by anyone, only unmodifiable.
`docs/concepts.rst` states the two-layer design the rest of the code follows: a signer signs bytes, and a serializer wraps a signer so non-bytes data can be signed.
The `secret_key` is what makes a signature unforgeable; the `salt` is a non-secret extra input that separates contexts (an 'activate' token must not validate as an 'upgrade' token).
open_questions: What exactly is the string after the dot, and how is it computed from the key?
How does a dict become the `eyJpZCI6...` part before signing?
Why does the plain `Serializer` produce `[1, 2, 3, 4].r7R9...` while `URLSafeSerializer` produces `WzEsMiwzLDRd.wSPH...` for the same input?

chapters.title: The Vocabulary of Failure
inputs: The idea that verification can fail (ch1)
facts: `BadData` is the root of every exception the library defines; it stores `message` and returns it from `__str__`.
`BadSignature` adds `payload`: the part of the token that failed verification, deliberately kept so callers can inspect (carefully) what was tampered with.

`BadTimeSignature` extends `BadSignature` with `date_signed`, a timezone-aware `datetime` since 2.0; `SignatureExpired` is a subclass of it with no extra members — the class itself is the signal that a token was valid but too old.

`BadPayload` descends directly from `BadData`, not `BadSignature`: a payload that deserializes badly is a different category from a payload that was tampered with, and it carries `original_error` so the underlying `json`/`zlib` failure isn't lost.
`BadHeader` exists with `header` and `original_error` fields but no code in this repository raises it; it is a leftover of the removed JWS support, kept because it is part of the public API.
open_questions: Who constructs `BadSignature` with a `payload`, and what exactly goes in it?
Who fills in `date_signed`, and how can a timestamp be recovered from a token whose signature is invalid?
If nothing raises `BadHeader`, why is it still exported?

chapters.title: Everything Is Bytes
facts: `want_bytes` is the library's universal front door: any `str` is UTF-8 encoded, `bytes` pass through unchanged. Almost every public method calls it first, which is why signing a `str` and signing its UTF-8 bytes give identical tokens.
`base64_encode` uses `base64.urlsafe_b64encode` and then strips all trailing `=` padding, so encoded values never contain characters that need escaping in a URL.

`base64_decode` re-adds the padding with `b'=' * (-len(string) % 4)`, decodes with `errors='ignore'` on the ASCII step, and converts any `TypeError`/`ValueError` into `BadData('Invalid base64-encoded data')` — this is the one place in `encoding.py` that raises a library exception.
`_base64_alphabet` is the byte string of letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `=` — the full set of characters that can appear in an encoded signature.

`int_to_bytes` packs an int with a big-endian 8-byte `struct.Struct('>Q')` and strips leading NUL bytes, so small numbers become short strings (0 becomes `b''`); `bytes_to_int` right-justifies back to 8 bytes before unpacking. `test_int_bytes` pins 0, 192 and 2**64-1 as round-trip cases.
open_questions: Why does the library need a compact integer encoding at all?
What is `_base64_alphabet` for, given nothing here validates against it?

chapters.title: Three Ways to Make a Signature
facts: `SigningAlgorithm` defines the whole plug-in surface: `get_signature(key, value)` raises `NotImplementedError`, and `verify_signature` is implemented once for everyone as `hmac.compare_digest(sig, self.get_signature(key, value))` — a constant-time comparison, so subclasses get timing-safe verification for free.
`HMACAlgorithm` builds `hmac.new(key, msg=value, digestmod=self.digest_method)` and returns the raw digest bytes (not base64 — that happens a layer up).
`NoneAlgorithm` returns `b''`; because verification still goes through `compare_digest`, an unsigned token validates trivially. It exists for tests and for formats that carry no signature.

`_lazy_sha1` wraps `hashlib.sha1` in a function and is installed as `staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)` for `default_digest_method`, so SHA-1 is never looked up at import time — on a FIPS build where SHA-1 is unavailable, importing itsdangerous still works and the developer can swap the default before first use.

`_make_keys_list` normalizes the `secret_key` argument once: a lone `str`/`bytes` becomes a one-element list, any other iterable is mapped through `want_bytes`. Both `Signer` and `Serializer` call it, which is how key rotation enters both layers identically.
open_questions: Where does the `key` passed to `get_signature` come from — is it the raw secret key?
Why is the algorithm object separate from the signer at all?

chapters.title: The Signer's Key: Salt, Separator, Derivation
facts: `Signer.__init__` stores `secret_keys` (a list, oldest to newest) and exposes `secret_key` as a property returning `secret_keys[-1]` — the newest key is always the signing key.

The separator is validated immediately: if `self.sep in _base64_alphabet`, a `ValueError` is raised, because a separator that can occur inside a base64 signature would make `rsplit` ambiguous. That's why `sep='-'` is rejected and `.` is the default.
`salt` defaults to `b'itsdangerous.Signer'`, and an explicit `None` falls back to that same default rather than to an empty salt.

`derive_key` never uses the secret key directly; it mixes salt and key by one of four schemes: `concat` (`digest(salt + key)`), `django-concat` (`digest(salt + b'signer' + key)`, the default, for Django cookie compatibility), `hmac` (HMAC of the salt keyed by the secret), and `none` (return the key unchanged). Anything else raises `TypeError('Unknown key derivation method')`.

The docstring is explicit that key derivation is not password stretching — it exists to separate contexts, which is why two serializers with different salts produce different signatures for the same payload (`docs/concepts.rst`).
open_questions: `derive_key` defaults to the newest key, but takes a `secret_key` parameter — who passes an older one?
How does a serializer reuse this constructor for fallback signers with different digest methods?

chapters.title: sign, unsign, and the Rotation Loop
facts: `get_signature` is the composition of the previous two chapters: `want_bytes(value)` → `derive_key()` → `algorithm.get_signature(key, value)` → `base64_encode`. The base64 step is what keeps tokens printable.
`sign` returns `value + self.sep + self.get_signature(value)`; the signature always covers exactly the bytes to its left.

`verify_signature` is where key rotation pays off: it decodes the candidate signature (returning `False` if base64 decoding throws at all) and then loops `for secret_key in reversed(self.secret_keys)`, deriving a key per secret and asking the algorithm — newest key first, oldest last.

`unsign` raises `BadSignature(f'No {sep!r} found in value')` if there is no separator, otherwise `rsplit(sep, 1)` splits at the *last* separator so payloads may contain the separator themselves. On mismatch it raises `BadSignature(..., payload=value)` — this is the `payload` attribute promised in chapter 2.
`validate` is just `unsign` with the exception swallowed into a bool.

`test_signer.py` pins the behaviours: a mutated value fails, a replaced separator fails, `sep='-'` raises `ValueError`, all four derivations round-trip, a custom `_ReverseAlgorithm` works, and a token signed with `Signer('a')` still validates under `Signer(['a', 'b'])`.
open_questions: This only signs bytes — how does `{'id': 5}` get in here?
Where does a timestamp fit into a format where the signature covers everything to its left?
answers: Chapter 5's question about passing an older `secret_key` to `derive_key`: `verify_signature` does it, once per rotation candidate.

chapters.title: Wrapping the Signer: Payloads
facts: A `Serializer` is configured entirely in `__init__`: `secret_keys` via the same `_make_keys_list`, a `salt` defaulting to `b'itsdangerous'` (note: different from the `Signer` default, so a bare `Signer` and a bare `Serializer` produce different signatures), a data serializer, a `Signer` *class* plus `signer_kwargs`, and a list of `fallback_signers`.
`default_serializer` is the stdlib `json` module itself — any object with `dumps`/`loads` can be substituted, which is how the test suite swaps in `pickle`.

`is_text_serializer` answers 'does this serializer produce `str` or `bytes`?' by actually calling `serializer.dumps({})` once and checking `isinstance(..., str)`. The answer is cached on the instance at construction time.
`dump_payload` is `want_bytes(self.serializer.dumps(obj, **self.serializer_kwargs))` — the payload handed to the signer is always bytes, whichever kind of serializer is configured.

`load_payload` mirrors it: decode to UTF-8 first if the serializer is a text one, then call `loads`, and wrap *any* exception in `BadPayload(..., original_error=e)`. A serializer can be passed per-call to override the instance's one, in which case `is_text_serializer` is recomputed for it.
`salt=None` is preserved as `None` rather than coerced, so that the signer's own default salt is used instead.
open_questions: `fallback_signers` is stored but unused so far — what shapes can its items take and when are they tried?
Why call `dumps({})` to detect text-ness instead of declaring it?
answers: Chapter 6's question about how non-bytes data is signed: it is serialized to bytes by `dump_payload` before the signer ever sees it.

chapters.title: dumps, loads, and the Parade of Unsigners
facts: `make_signer` instantiates `self.signer(self.secret_keys, salt=salt, **self.signer_kwargs)` — it hands over the whole key list, so the signer does rotation internally as in chapter 6.

`dumps` is three lines that summarize the library: `dump_payload` → `make_signer(salt).sign(payload)` → decode to `str` if the data serializer was a text one. This is why `Serializer.dumps` returns `str` by default but `bytes` with, say, a pickle serializer.

`iter_unsigners` yields the primary signer first, then builds one signer per fallback entry. Each entry may be a dict of kwargs (reusing `self.signer`), a `Signer` subclass (reusing `self.signer_kwargs`), or a `(class, kwargs)` tuple — the three forms documented in `docs/serializer.rst`.

Fallback signers are constructed per secret key (`for secret_key in self.secret_keys: yield fallback(secret_key, ...)`), unlike the primary signer which receives the whole list at once — so a rotated key set multiplies the number of fallback attempts.

`loads` coerces to bytes, then tries every unsigner in order, returning `self.load_payload(signer.unsign(s))` on the first success, remembering the last `BadSignature` and re-raising it if all fail. A `BadPayload` from `load_payload` is *not* caught, so it escapes immediately.
The `salt` argument on `dumps`/`loads` overrides the instance salt per call, which is how one serializer can serve several contexts.
open_questions: `loads` raises on a bad signature — but chapter 2 said the payload is preserved. How does a caller get at it?
If a fallback signer exists, does an *expired* token get retried against the fallbacks?
answers: Chapter 7's question about `fallback_signers`: `iter_unsigners` interprets the three accepted shapes and yields them after the primary signer.

chapters.title: Reading Tokens You Don't Trust
inputs: `loads`, `load_payload` and the exception hierarchy (ch7, ch8, ch2)
facts: `loads_unsafe` never raises: it returns `(signature_valid, payload)`. It delegates to `_loads_unsafe_impl`, which is the extension point subclasses use to inject extra arguments.

`_loads_unsafe_impl` first tries `loads`. On `BadSignature` it checks `e.payload`: `None` means there was nothing recoverable (e.g. the separator was missing), so it returns `(False, None)`; otherwise it calls `load_payload` on the tampered bytes and returns `(False, value)` — and if *that* raises `BadPayload`, it returns `(False, None)`.
The docs are blunt about the risk: this path deserializes data known to be tampered with, which is why `load_payload` is a separate explicit step ('think pickle instead of json!').

`dump`, `load` and `load_unsafe` are thin file wrappers over `dumps`/`loads`/`loads_unsafe`; the file object must match the serializer's text-or-bytes nature, which the tests handle by picking `StringIO` or `BytesIO` based on `isinstance(serializer.dumps(value), bytes)`.
open_questions: How does a caller (or a type checker) know whether `dumps` will hand them `str` or `bytes` before running the code?
answers: Chapter 8's question about retrieving the payload after a failed signature check: `BadSignature.payload` plus an explicit `load_payload`, or the packaged `loads_unsafe`.

chapters.title: Making the Return Type Honest
facts: `Serializer` is `t.Generic[_TSerialized]`, where `_TSerialized` is a `TypeVar` bound to `str | bytes`; under `TYPE_CHECKING` it is declared via `typing_extensions.TypeVar` with `default=str | bytes`, so bare `Serializer` still means something to newer checkers.

`_PDataSerializer` is a structural `Protocol` with positional-only `loads`/`dumps`, letting the stdlib `json` module, `pickle`, and `_CompactJSON` all satisfy the same static contract without inheritance.

Five `__init__` overloads encode the inference rules: no serializer → `Serializer[str]`; a `_PDataSerializer[bytes]` positionally or by keyword → `Serializer[bytes]`; and two `t.Any` fallbacks for serializers whose signature (extra kwargs) doesn't structurally match the strict protocol, in which case the user must annotate the type themselves.

`is_text_serializer` is annotated as returning `te.TypeGuard[_PDataSerializer[str]]`, narrowing the serializer type inside `load_payload`'s text branch; a comment notes `TypeIs` would be the better tool once available.

The runtime `__init__` accepts `serializer: t.Any | None` — all the precision is static, and `# type: ignore` comments in `dumps`/`load_payload` mark the two places where the runtime `is_text_serializer` flag outruns what the checker can prove.
open_questions: How does a subclass replace `default_signer` with an incompatible type without breaking this generic machinery?
answers: Chapter 9's question about knowing the token type statically: the generic parameter plus overloads make `dumps`'s return type follow from the serializer argument.

Chapter 7's question about detecting text-ness by calling `dumps({})`: the runtime probe is paired with a static `TypeGuard`, because a Protocol can't declare which of `str`/`bytes` a duck-typed module returns.

chapters.title: Adding the Clock
facts: `TimestampSigner.sign` inserts a field: `value + sep + base64(int_to_bytes(get_timestamp()))`, and *then* signs that whole thing. The signature therefore covers the timestamp, so a forged expiry date breaks the signature.
`get_timestamp` returns `int(time.time())` — a plain Unix timestamp since 1.0; `timestamp_to_datetime` converts it to a timezone-aware UTC `datetime` (naive datetimes were dropped in 2.0).

`unsign` deliberately catches the parent's `BadSignature` instead of letting it fly, keeping `sig_error` and falling back to `e.payload` — because even an invalid token may contain a readable timestamp worth reporting to the user.

Failure ordering is careful: no separator in the result → re-raise the original signature error if there was one, else `BadTimeSignature('timestamp missing')`; a signature error with a parseable timestamp → `BadTimeSignature(str(sig_error), payload=value, date_signed=ts_dt)`; a good signature with an unparseable timestamp → `BadTimeSignature('Malformed timestamp')`.

`timestamp_to_datetime` is wrapped in `except (ValueError, OSError, OverflowError)` because a huge timestamp raises `OSError` on Windows and `OverflowError` on 32-bit builds — these become `BadTimeSignature('Malformed timestamp')` rather than escaping as unrelated errors.

With `max_age` set, `age = get_timestamp() - ts_int`; `age > max_age` raises `SignatureExpired('Signature age N > M seconds')`, and `age < 0` *also* raises `SignatureExpired`, so a token from the future is rejected rather than silently accepted (changed in 2.0).
The two `@t.overload` declarations make `return_timestamp` switch the return type between `bytes` and `tuple[bytes, datetime]`.
open_questions: How does a serializer expose the timestamp to `loads` callers, and what happens to the other fallback signers when one reports expiry?
answers: Chapter 6's question about where a timestamp fits: it is appended as another `sep`-delimited field *inside* the signed region.
Chapter 3's question about compact integers: `int_to_bytes` strips leading NULs so the base64 timestamp field stays short in every token.
Chapter 2's question about `date_signed`: `TimestampSigner.unsign` fills it, even on the failure paths, by parsing the timestamp field after splitting.

chapters.title: TimedSerializer: Expiry Wins
facts: `TimedSerializer` subclasses `Serializer[_TSerialized]` and changes exactly one thing declaratively: `default_signer = TimestampSigner` (with a `# pyright: ignore` because the attribute type is narrowed relative to the base class).
`iter_unsigners` is overridden only to re-cast the iterator type; the construction logic from chapter 8 is untouched, so fallback signers work the same way.

`loads` re-declares its signature as `(s, max_age=None, return_timestamp=False, salt=None)` — `salt` moved to fourth position for backwards compatibility, which is why the override needs `# type: ignore[override]` and a TODO comment.
It always calls the signer with `return_timestamp=True`, loads the payload, and then decides whether to hand the timestamp back to the caller based on its own `return_timestamp` flag.

The crucial control-flow choice: `SignatureExpired` is re-raised immediately inside the loop, *before* the generic `BadSignature` handler, so a token that verified correctly but is too old never gets retried against fallback signers or older keys.
`loads_unsafe` reuses `_loads_unsafe_impl` from chapter 9, threading `max_age` through `load_kwargs` — which is precisely why that helper takes a kwargs dict.
open_questions: These tokens still contain raw JSON and can be long — how do they become short and URL-safe?
answers: Chapter 8's question about expired tokens and fallbacks: expiry short-circuits the unsigner loop.
Chapter 11's question about surfacing the timestamp: `loads(..., return_timestamp=True)` returns `(payload, datetime)`.
Chapter 10's question about overriding `default_signer`: it is done with a narrowing annotation plus a targeted checker suppression.

chapters.title: Short and URL-Safe
facts: `_CompactJSON` is a two-static-method wrapper over `json` that defaults `ensure_ascii=False` and `separators=(',', ':')`, removing every byte of whitespace and avoiding `\uXXXX` bloat for non-ASCII text.
`URLSafeSerializerMixin` sets `default_serializer = _CompactJSON` and overrides only the two payload methods — signing, key handling, fallbacks and timing are all inherited unchanged.

`dump_payload` calls `super().dump_payload`, zlib-compresses the result, and keeps the compressed form only `if len(compressed) < len(json) - 1` — the `- 1` pays for the marker byte. A compressed payload is prefixed with `.` after base64 encoding.

`load_payload` reverses it: a leading `.` means decompress; base64 decoding failure becomes `BadPayload('Could not base64 decode the payload...')` and zlib failure becomes `BadPayload('Could not zlib decompress...')`, each carrying `original_error`.

Because the payload is base64-encoded, the only non-alphanumeric characters in a finished token are `-`, `_` and `.` — and `.` is safe as the separator precisely because of the `_base64_alphabet` check from chapter 5 (which forbids `-`, `_` and `=`).

`URLSafeSerializer` is `class URLSafeSerializer(URLSafeSerializerMixin, Serializer[str])` and `URLSafeTimedSerializer` is the same mixin over `TimedSerializer[str]`, both with empty bodies: the entire feature is MRO composition. The mixin's own base, `Serializer[str]`, makes `super()` resolve to whichever concrete serializer is later in the MRO.
open_questions: Four serializer classes now share overlapping behaviour — how is each combination actually verified?
answers: Chapter 1's question about why `URLSafeSerializer` produces a different-looking token: the payload is compact-JSON, optionally zlib-compressed, and base64-encoded before signing.
Chapter 12's question about short URL-safe tokens: this mixin, layered onto either `Serializer` or `TimedSerializer`.

chapters.title: The Test Suite as a Mirror of the Class Tree
inputs: All four serializer classes and both signer classes (ch6, ch11, ch8, ch12, ch13)
facts: The test classes inherit along the same lines as the source classes: `TestTimestampSigner(FreezeMixin, TestSigner)` and `TestURLSafeTimedSerializer(TestURLSafeSerializer, TestTimedSerializer)`, so every base-class test re-runs against every subclass by simply overriding the `signer_factory`/`serializer_factory` fixture.

`TestSerializer.serializer_factory` is parametrized over `Serializer` and `partial(Serializer, serializer=pickle)`, so the whole suite runs twice — once with a text serializer and once with a bytes one. The `coerce_str` helper exists solely to write mutations that work for both.

`FreezeMixin` uses `freezegun` to pin time to 2011-06-24 and exposes the `freeze` handle so tests can `tick()` past `max_age`; `test_future_age` jumps backwards to 1971 to exercise the negative-age branch from chapter 11.
`TestURLSafeSerializer` parametrizes `value` with `'a' * 1000` (id `zlib`) to force the compression branch of `dump_payload`.

`test_iter_unsigners` asserts the exact ordering and construction of fallbacks: the first unsigner still uses `_lazy_sha1`, and all subsequent ones — from a kwargs dict, a `(class, kwargs)` tuple, and a bare subclass — use SHA-256.

`test_digests` pins literal output strings (`'[42].-9cNi0CxsSB3hZPNCe9a2eEs1ZM'` for SHA-1, a long SHA-512 value) so that any accidental change to the default digest or key derivation breaks the build — these are the library's compatibility anchors.
open_questions: How is all of this packaged, type-checked and released so downstreams like Flask can rely on it?
answers: Chapter 13's question about verifying the combinations: the test hierarchy mirrors the class hierarchy and reuses fixtures.

chapters.title: Shipping It
inputs: The whole package and its test suite (ch1-ch14)
facts: The package has no runtime dependencies at all — only stdlib `json`, `hashlib`, `hmac`, `base64`, `struct`, `zlib`, `time` — which is why it can sit underneath Flask's session handling.

Build is `flit_core` with `[tool.flit.module] name = 'itsdangerous'`; the empty `src/itsdangerous/py.typed` marker is what makes the inline annotations from chapter 10 visible to downstream type checkers.

Typing is enforced three ways in the `typing` tox env: `mypy` in `strict` mode over `src`, `pyright` in standard mode, and `pyright --verifytypes itsdangerous --ignoreexternal`, which checks that the *public* API is fully annotated — the reason for the careful overloads and `TypeGuard`.

`filterwarnings = ['error']` in the pytest config turns any warning into a test failure, and the CI matrix runs CPython 3.10-3.13 plus PyPy on Linux, Windows and macOS — the platforms behind the `OSError`/`OverflowError` handling in chapter 11.

`CHANGES.rst` records why the code looks as it does: JWS serializers were deprecated in 2.0 and removed in 2.1 (leaving `BadHeader` behind), simplejson support was dropped in favour of the `serializer=` argument, key rotation arrived in 2.0, and the lazy SHA-1 default was introduced in 2.2 for FIPS builds.
The 2.3.0 entry in progress drops Python 3.8/3.9 and removes previously deprecated code, matching `requires-python = '>=3.10'`.
answers: Chapter 2's question about `BadHeader`: it survives as public API from the removed JWS serializers, documented in `CHANGES.rst`.
Chapter 14's question about packaging and release: flit + `py.typed` + a three-tool typing gate + a cross-platform CI matrix.
